endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Research models/solutions typically require IRB assessment and approval prior to development or deployment.

endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: Health systems may find that AI is increasingly “seeping in” as vendors incorporate it into existing workflows.

endorsements.title: The EU AI Act: implications and compliance guidance for healthcare facilities
endorsements.quote: This process extends beyond obvious clinical applications, such as diagnostic imaging or predictive analytics, to include AI within electronic health records (EHRs), administrative workflows, and patient engagement platforms.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether inventorying and risk-categorizing AI embedded in enterprise platforms and legacy products improves governance or patient outcomes, and no study documents the hazard itself. Support rests on three sources, one framework, one guidance document and one commentary, that describe the problem or call for the practice without measuring its effect.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three endorsements are expert opinion. The CHAI quotation concerns IRB review of research models, which bears only indirectly on inventorying vendor-enabled features already in production.

The EU AI Act commentary advises that compliance review should extend to AI within EHRs, administrative workflows and patient engagement platforms. This suggests an inventory may serve as a first step toward risk classification under that statute. The commentary interprets legal obligations and does not report whether inventories improve compliance in practice.

The delivery-system guidance reports that AI is "seeping in" as vendors add it to existing workflows, which implies that procurement review alone may miss these features. No source supplied here estimates the staff time, cost or vendor cooperation needed to build and maintain such an inventory at scale.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how often vendor-enabled AI features operate without governance awareness, and that compare health systems with and without a maintained inventory on outcomes such as time to detect newly activated features, share of features receiving risk review, and downstream safety events. Estimates of the labor and vendor-disclosure burden of keeping an inventory current would also inform adoption decisions.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer governance staff to build an inventory, and whether the practice performs similarly in those settings is unknown.
